headline: Funding flows. Launches fail. Defense partners up.
deck: This week highlights funding successes amid launch failures and new defense collaborations.

stories.head: Northrop Grumman teams with Apex for interceptors
stories.body: Northrop Grumman has partnered with Apex to develop space-based interceptors for the Golden Dome program, marking another chapter in defense contracting. While the exact financial terms remain under wraps, Apex recently raised $95 million in a Series C round, which likely helps grease the wheels for this collaboration. This partnership could position them as key players in the growing space-based defense sector.
stories.soWhat: Defense contractors are getting cozy, but the real question is whether this will lead to actual capabilities or just more PowerPoint slides.

stories.head: Spaceport bonds become law, changing financing game
stories.body: New legislation has officially made spaceport facility bonds law, potentially reshaping how we finance space infrastructure. This could open up a $1 billion market for spaceports, as companies look to capitalize on this new funding mechanism. The implications for private spaceports are significant, as they may now attract more investment without the usual financial hurdles.
stories.soWhat: If spaceports get funded like municipal projects, we might see a boom in launches—if only someone could figure out how to launch without blowing things up first.

stories.head: New Glenn failure tightens already strained launch market
stories.body: The explosion of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket has exacerbated an already constrained launch market, which was already feeling the pinch from increasing competition. With the launch market tightening further, companies are scrambling to find reliable alternatives. The failure comes at a time when SpaceX continues to dominate, leaving others to ponder their next moves.
stories.soWhat: In a market where reliability is king, Blue Origin's misstep could mean more contracts for SpaceX and a longer road to recovery for competitors.

watchlist.title: True Anomaly's Series C implications
watchlist.body: With True Anomaly raising $190 million, watch for increased focus on co-orbital security solutions as the DoD pushes for more robust defense technologies.

watchlist.title: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser next steps
watchlist.body: Having cleared its critical design review, Sierra Space's Dream Chaser will now have to prove it can deliver without becoming another cautionary tale in the industry.

watchlist.title: China's launch frequency to watch
watchlist.body: China's recent launches show no signs of slowing down; keep an eye on how this affects U.S. market dynamics and procurement strategies.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN extension impact
watchlist.body: Palantir's $480 million extension on the TITAN program signals confidence in ground station capabilities, likely influencing future defense tech investments.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
